paper_title: Simulator-as-Proxy World Model for Robot Manipulation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Video world models for robots are increasingly conditioned on a simulated or rendered proxy of the scene, on the assumption that the video will show what the proxy shows. Testing this assumption requires a proxy whose state is explicit and can be perturbed. We present SimPWM (Simulator-as-Proxy World Model): given a calibrated camera, it represents, from the first frame alone, the robot by its 3D model and the objects the gripper may touch as 3D points; a rule-based simulator with no trained parameters moves them under the actions, and a video model renders the result. SimPWM returns the realistic video together with the simulated state. We then freeze the simulated objects while the arm moves as recorded and check whether the video still shows the object lifted. On DROID episodes from unseen setups, the answer differs for the arm and for the objects. With each of three base video models, the arm follows the proxy (robot IoU 0.75-0.78, against at most 0.69 for end-to-end models); rendering the robot alone already gives this. What the simulated objects add is the object state: against a robot-only proxy, they cut missed pick-ups from 54% to 38%, and the video follows them only with some base models: on rigid objects, freezing them lowers the lift rate of MiniMax-H3, fine-tuned on episodes whose simulation agrees with the real video, from 42% to 10%, but that of LTX-2.3, trained on the same episodes, only from 57% to 49%, as if it inferred the grasp from the arm motion; more than half of the remaining lifts of MiniMax-H3 are of cloth and rope, which the simulator carries rigidly. With any base model, the simulated state records what the simulation did; under perturbed actions, a video that disagrees with it reveals that the video ignores the simulated state.

sections.title:
1 Introduction
Action-conditioned video world models take an observation and a sequence of robot actions and render
the future (Yang et al., 2024b; NVIDIA et al., 2025b; Zhu et al., 2025). They must follow the actions
strictly: the arm must move exactly as commanded, an object may move only when the gripper grasps
it, and it must stay where it is released. To this end they are increasingly conditioned on a simulated or
rendered proxy of the scene, such as the commanded robot rendered from its model (Kim et al., 2026), a
4D occupancy sequence (Yang et al., 2026), structural controls such as depth (NVIDIA et al., 2025a) or a
physics simulation (Liu et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025b), on the assumption that the video will show what the
proxy shows. Testing this assumption requires a proxy whose state is explicit and can be perturbed. Fig. 1
does so: with the simulated cup frozen while the arm moves as recorded, one video model leaves the cup in
place, as the proxy does, and another still lifts it.

Under the recorded actions (top), both base models lift the cup as the proxy does. With the gripper held open (middle) or the simulated objects frozen while the arm moves as recorded (bottom), the proxy leaves the cup in place; SimPWM-H3-C does too, whereas SimPWM-LTX-2.3-C still lifts it. Figure 2: SimPWM outputs: realistic video and explicit simulated state. SimPWM-H3-C carries the cup as in the real video; Ctrl-World loses it and Agentic Real2Sim (render composited on the input background) knocks it over. Such proxy also combines the strengths of the two current kinds of models, which fail in opposite ways  (Fig. 2)  . End-to-end video world models (Zhu et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2026; NVIDIA et al., 2025b) focus mostly on visual quality: their frames look realistic, but they often do not follow the actions. The arm drifts from the commanded trajectory, and grasped objects split, stay behind or dissolve. Because the consequence is never represented, these errors are hard to detect or correct. Simulators compute the consequences from kinematics and contact, but they need scene. scene rebuilt from real image, by hand, automatically (Ranawaka et al., 2026) or by agents (Chen et al., 2026), does not match it exactly, and few centimetres decide whether grasp succeeds; rigid-body physics also mishandles ropes and cloth, and the rendered video does not look real. We combine the two into model that returns two outputs: realistic video from video model, and an explicit state of what the actions cause, from simulator, that the video can be tested against. What moves where (the arm, the grasped object and where it goes) depends mainly on coarse geometry and the commanded motion, which simple simulator computes explicitly. How it looks, from appearance and shadows to how rope or cloth hangs  (Fig. 3)  , depends on fine physics and appearance, which video models learn well from data. Accordingly, we credit arm following to the robot rendering, which prior work also uses (Kim et al., 2026), and evaluate the simulator only on what it adds: which object moves, and whether the video follows it. Our model, SimPWM (Simulator-as-Proxy World Model), is built on this split  (Fig. 4)  . From the first frame it separates the scene into three parts, the robot as its 3D model, the objects the gripper may touch as 3D points, and the background (real-to-sim); simple simulator moves the robot and the objects under the actions with explicit rules for grasp, carry, release and gravity  (Fig. 5)  ; and the simulated scene is rendered per frame as proxy: the first frame, with the robot and every moved object redrawn where the simulator puts them. video model that takes reference video, fine-tuned to render such proxies, turns them into realistic video (sim-to-real ); we instantiate it with three base models, MiniMax-H3, LTX-2.3 and Cosmos-Transfer 2.5. For manipulation, Ctrl-World and WorldGym roll out and rank policies (Guo et al., 2026; Quevedo et al., 2026), RoboScape adds depth and keypoint objectives (Shang et al., 2025), EnerVerse-AC projects end-effector actions into the image (Jiang et al., 2025b), and DreamDojo pretrains on human video with latent actions (Gao et al., 2026). These models are trained end to end, so the effect of an action is implicit in the weights. Other models learn how the 3D scene moves, as particles, scene flow, point flows or voxel latents (Whitney et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026); SimPWM computes it with rules that need no training (we compare with PointWorld in Secs. 4.3 and 4.4). Physics and proxies for video generation. Closest to our approach  (Table 1)  are methods that drive video generator with physics simulation of single image (Liu et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025b); SimPWM shares this split but simulates robot: its inputs are joint and gripper commands, it decides grasps rather than applying forces, and it needs no material estimation. Video can also be rendered from structural conditions such as label maps, depth, edges or masks (Wang et al., 2018; Mallya et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2023; Esser et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023; Guo et al., 2024; NVIDIA et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2025a) or 3D tracking videos (Gu et al., 2025), for robots from 4D occupancy (Yang et al., 2026) or render of the commanded robot (Kim et al., 2026). These conditions are given, extracted from reference video, or cover only the robot; in SimPWM they are simulated at test time from the first frame and the actions, so they encode what the actions do to objects. Our robot-only proxy is the closest analogue of RoFacto (Secs. 4.4 and 4.5). Real-to-sim. Evaluating policies in simulation requires matching the simulated scene to the real one (Li et al., 2024). Agentic Real2Sim turns DROID recording into MuJoCo twin with vision-language agents (Chen et al., 2026); others build scenes or objects from videos or scans (Torne et al., 2024; Ranawaka et al., 2026; Jiang et al., 2025a; Yu et al., 2025). These need recorded videos or scans, and their scenes need not match the image; SimPWM lifts an image-aligned point set from the first frame, poses the robot with MuJoCo (Todorov et al., 2012), and leaves appearance to the video model.

sections.title: 3.1 Real-to-Sim
sections.content: Metric depth. On DROID the external camera is stereo camera: we estimate disparity on the rectified first-frame pair with FoundationStereo (Wen et al., 2025) and convert it to metric depth with the focal length and baseline. Pixels without stereo support, such as the border that only one camera sees and occlusions, take monocular metric depth from Depth Anything V2 (Yang et al., 2024a), scaled to the stereo depth by the median ratio on the valid non-robot pixels. Without stereo pair (Sec. 4.3), the monocular depth is used alone, scaled with the robot as ruler. Support and objects. The support is gravity-aligned plane fitted by RANSAC to the non-robot points; among strong horizontal candidates we take the one closest to the lowest point that the effector reaches during the actions. Objects are what rises above the support. We segment them with SAM 2 (Ravi et al., 2025) and SAM 3 (Carion et al., 2026) proposals, split large holes in the support with SAM 2 point prompts, and add segment at every point where the gripper closes. Action-conditioned depth refinement (action snap). For each window in which the gripper closes, we project the lowest effector pose into the first frame; if that pixel lies on an object, the object must be at the effectors depth there. Scaling the objects points about the camera centre by factor leaves its image footprint unchanged, so we choose to match the two depths (within [0.35, 2.5]).

When the gripper closes and holds nothing, it grasps the object that fits between the open jaws and has the most points, at least k, between its pads; an object wider than the jaws (e.g. cloth) is pinched at its edge. 5 Carry. sections.title: 3.3 Sim-to-Real
sections.content: Figure 5: Rule-based point simulator: grasp, rigid carry, release with gravity, and the pad distance (diagnostic only). Proxy rendering. Each frame of the simulated scene is rendered into the proxy: the robot from its posed mesh, the objects as point splats and the background from the first-frame depth. The video model receives the RGB proxy, in which every point keeps its first-frame colour and the robot is shaded mesh; where the robot or held object uncovers part of its first-frame footprint, the first frame shows nothing, and we fill these pixels with marker colour (magenta). The same rendering gives depth map (the depth proxy, compared in Sec. 4.4) and semantic map, in which only the robot and the objects that the gripper held get their own label; the latter is not an input to the video model, but gives the readout: whether, and which object, the gripper holds at each step (Sec. 4.5). Video model. The proxy fixes where the robot is and where the simulator moves each object in every frame. The video model supplies the rest: appearance, lighting and shadows, the background hidden in the first frame, and the physical detail that the simulator lacks, such as how rope or cloth hangs. Any video model that takes reference video can render the proxy; we fine-tune three, each receiving the proxy as the reference video, the real first frame x0 and text prompt naming the task. SimPWM-H3 is LoRA (rank 32) on MiniMax-H3 (MiniMax, 2026) (33B parameters), whose Ref2VA variant also takes x0 as reference image and as the first latent frame of the target; it generates 158 frames at 24 fps, to which the 97 recorded steps are resampled (so clip lasts 6.5 instead of 6.4 s). SimPWM-LTX-2.3 is an in-context LoRA (IC-LoRA) (Huang et al., 2024) on LTX-2.3 (22B), an update of LTX-2 (HaCohen et al., 2026), generating 97 frames at 15 fps. SimPWM-Cosmos-Transfer is control branch on Cosmos-Transfer 2.5 (NVIDIA et al., 2025c) (2.4B), trained like SimPWM-LTX-2.3. All three are trained on the 3,000 training episodes of Sec. 4.1. Our main model, SimPWM-H3-C, is trained in the same way on the consistent subset: the 845 training episodes whose proxy agrees with the real video; SimPWM-LTX-2.3-C is LTX-2.3 trained on it for comparison. H3 zero-shot is MiniMax-H3 with our proxy and no fine-tuning; the ablation models are SimPWM-H3-C at 640352, one per proxy variant. Table A1 lists all variants.

sections.title: 4.2 Comparison
sections.content: DROID. Table 2 compares SimPWM with the three baselines on the DROID test episodes with the metrics of Sec. 4.1; Figs. 2, 3 and 6 show examples. The rendered robot makes the difference for the arm (Sec. 4.4 isolates it): whatever their base model, the fine-tuned SimPWM variants give the lowest image error (PSNR, LPIPS) and follow the commanded motion most closely, whereas the end-to-end models drift from the commanded arm, DreamDojo most. With the same base family, data and training steps, SimPWM-Cosmos-Transfer nearly doubles the robot IoU of Cosmos-Predict 2.5, so the gain comes from the proxy rather than from larger model. SimPWM-H3-C gives the lowest image error and FVD, level with SimPWM-H3: the consistent subset costs no image quality. Given our proxy without fine-tuning, MiniMax-H3 already follows the arm more closely than the end-to-end models, but fine-tuning improves image quality and arm following (FVD 194.1 85.6, robot IoU 0.718 0.777). Ctrl-World scores highest on Physics-IQ, which counts every changing pixel; the SimPWM-H3 models and SimPWM-Cosmos-Transfer come close, whereas the output of SimPWM-LTX-2.3 flickers slightly in static regions. Other robots. With LTX-2.3 retrained per robot, SimPWM ranks third of 19 models in trajectory accuracy on the bimanual WorldArena benchmark but is weaker in image quality, and on the GR1 humanoid it follows the arms more closely than DreamDojo (robot IoU 0.861 vs. 0.815) with better PSNR and SSIM but worse LPIPS and FVD (Sec. E).

The rows replace our calibration by the one DROID logs, stereo by monocular depth, or remove the action snap; all are scored on the same episodes and targets. Calibration matters most: with DROIDs logged calibration, the closing point lands beside the target and many right grasps become wrong. Without the action snap, grasp success changes little (69.5% vs. 67.6%, not significant), but the grasped objects are carried at an offset, since they stay at their first-frame depth: object IoU falls from 0.287 to 0.185. sections.title: 4.4 Sim-to-Real Evaluation

sections.title: 4.5 Following the Simulated State
sections.content: We take the 133 test episodes in which the real robot lifts an object (grasp judge of Table 4) and perturb the input so that it should not (Fig. 1 shows one episode, Fig. 8 the rates). Claude judge, blind to the method, sees the first frame and eight frames from the first stall of the gripper on and says whether the target is lifted; seeing only these, it confirms 68% of the lifts that the judge of Table 4 finds on the whole clip, so we compare its rates only across methods. blind human label agrees with it on 44 of 46 decided random sheets (κ = 0.91; Sec. C.4). Open gripper. With the gripper never closing (no close), SimPWM-H3-C shows lift in 16% of the videos, SimPWM-LTX-2.3-C in 44% (on rigid targets 11% vs. 39%; Table 5). 10 of the 21 lifts of SimPWM-H3-C are of deformable targets, whose shape the simulator does not model. The ablation models lift in 8% (RGB proxy) and 14% (robot only): the video follows the rendered gripper. Ctrl-World lifts even less (7%) but has no object state to freeze; DreamDojo lifts little under any actions, Cosmos-Predict 2.5 in 11% (31% when recorded). 10 Frozen objects. Freezing the simulated objects while the arm moves as recorded separates them from the gripper. SimPWM-H3-C lifts less often than SimPWM-LTX-2.3-C and the real videos (47%, 62% and 68% under the recorded actions): the simulator lifts an object in 90 of the 133 episodes, and SimPWM-H3-C shows the lift in 54% of these ([43, 64]) but in 30% of the other 43 (SimPWM-LTX-2.3-C 63% and 58%). It might thus merely be conservative; but conservative model would keep its rate when the objects are frozen. On the 96 rigid targets, SimPWM-H3-C drops from 42% to 10%, and SimPWM-LTX-2.3-C only from 57% to 49%  (Table 5)  ; over all 133 episodes, the paired difference of the drops is 22 points (95% CI [12, 31]). More than half of the remaining lifts of SimPWM-H3-C are of deformable targets (14 of 24), which the simulator carries rigidly. Freezing also closes the fingers fully when nothing is grasped, which the robot-only proxy isolates: in the ablation models it loses 12.8 points against 31.6 with the RGB proxy, so 18.8 points (95% CI [10, 28]) come from the simulated object state. In consistent training data, closing gripper that rises and lifted object Why base models differ. always occur together, so following the arm and following the simulated object fit the data equally well, and which one model learns is set by its prior. LTX-2.3 predicts moved objects mainly from the arm, which gives 91% of the proxys gain in their denoising loss. MiniMax-H3 follows the object state without fine-tuning (H3 zero-shot loses 63% of its lifts on rigid targets). Episodes that disagree with the simulation tip the balance towards the arm: trained on all 3,000 episodes (a quarter disagree on the grasp), SimPWM-H3 loses only 43% of its rigid-target lifts under frozen objects, against 75% for SimPWM-H3-C  (Table 5)  . SimPWM-Cosmos-Transfer, trained on the data of SimPWM-H3, loses 21%; on all 133 episodes its drop is 17 points ([8, 26]) below that of SimPWM-H3-C and close to those of SimPWM-LTX-2.3-C and SimPWM-H3. We hypothesise that the prior of MiniMax-H3 comes from its Ref2VA pretraining, which asks the output to follow reference video, whereas LTX-2.3 learns to use reference only in fine-tuning (details: Sec. C.4).

Does the video follow the simulated state? For the arm, yes, with each of three base video models; for
the objects, only if the prior of the base model favours the reference video (MiniMax-H3, possibly from
pretraining), whereas LTX-2.3 infers grasps from the arm motion. Consistent data alone cannot tell the
two apart, so our recipe is: fine-tune on consistent episodes and choose a base model that passes the
perturbation tests.
